history: To say ‘to speak’, French uses a word from the Church. Classical Latin said loqui. But the Christian Latin of late legal texts and saints' lives had a new verb, parabolare, built on parabola. Latin had taken parabola from Greek parabolḗ, ‘comparison’, and the Bible used it for the parables. The TLFi says the new verb won because it was fuller in form and more concrete in meaning than loqui. It is one of the oldest French words on record: the Jonas fragment, written between 937 and 952, already has parla, ‘he spoke’. Its family is close at hand: la parole, ‘the spoken word’, le parloir and le parlement. English borrowed the verb as well and still has parley, ‘a talk with an enemy’.
historyEinfach: Parler comes from Latin parabolare. This verb is made from parabola, a word that came from Greek and meant ‘comparison’ or ‘parable’, a story with a lesson. The old Latin verb for ‘to speak’ was loqui, but people preferred the new one. La parole and le parlement are in the same family.

elsewhere.text: English took the French verb in the Middle Ages. Today parley is a formal talk, often with an enemy.
